en: Majjhima Nikāya 115:
The Discourse on the Many Elements (Bahudhātuka Sutta) Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, whatever fears arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man.”
Whatever misfortunes arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man;
whatever calamities arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man.
Just as, monks, a fire released from a hut of reeds or a hut of grass burns even gabled houses—those plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with doors bolted and windows closed.
In the same way, monks, whatever fears arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man;
whatever calamities arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man;
whatever misfortunes arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man.
Thus, monks, the fool is full of fear, while the wise person is free from fear;
the fool is beset by calamity, while the wise person is free from calamity;
the fool is beset by misfortune, while the wise person is free from misfortune.
“Bhikkhus, there is no fear from the wise, no calamity from the wise, and no misfortune from the wise.
Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall be wise and investigative.’”
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
“To what extent, Bhante, is a wise bhikkhu fit to be called ‘investigative’?

“Ānanda, when a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and impossible—to that extent he is fit to be called ‘investigative.’”
“To this extent, Ānanda, a wise bhikkhu is fit to be called ‘investigative.
But to what extent, Bhante, is a bhikkhu fit to be called ‘skilled in the elements’?
“Ānanda, there are these eighteen elements:”
The eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element;
the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element;
The tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible-object element, and the body-consciousness element;
the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
“Ānanda, when one knows and sees these eighteen elements,
it is sufficient, Ānanda, to say that a bhikkhu is ‘skilled in the elements.
“But, Bhante, might there be another way in which it is sufficient to say that a bhikkhu is ‘skilled in the elements’?”
“It may be so, Ānanda.
There are these six elements, Ānanda:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.”
“Ānanda, when one knows and sees these six elements—
to this extent, Ānanda, it is sufficient to call a bhikkhu ‘skilled in the elements.
“But, Bhante, might there be another way in which it is sufficient to call a bhikkhu ‘skilled in the elements’?”
“It may be so, Ānanda.
There are these six elements, Ānanda:
the pleasure element, the pain element, the joy element, the grief element, the equanimity element, and the ignorance element.”
“Ānanda, when one knows and sees these six elements—
to this extent, Ānanda, it is sufficient to call a bhikkhu ‘skilled in the elements.
“But, Bhante, might there be another way in which it is sufficient to call a bhikkhu ‘skilled in the elements’?”
“It may be so, Ānanda.
There are these six elements, Ānanda:
the element of sensual desire, the element of renunciation, the element of ill will, the element of non-ill will, the element of cruelty, and the element of non-cruelty.”
“Ānanda, when one knows and sees these six elements—
by this much alone, Ānanda, it is sufficient to call a monk ‘skilled in the elements.
“But, Bhante, might there be another way in which it is sufficient to call a monk ‘skilled in the elements’?”
“It may be so, Ānanda.
There are these three elements, Ānanda:
the element of sensual desire, the element of form, and the element of the formless.”
“Ānanda, when one knows and sees these three elements,
it is sufficient, to that extent, to call a bhikkhu ‘skilled in the elements.
“But, Bhante, might there be another way in which it is sufficient to call a bhikkhu ‘skilled in the elements’?”
“It may be so, Ānanda.
There are these two elements, Ānanda:
the conditioned element and the unconditioned element.”
"These, Ānanda, are the two elements from which one knows and sees.
To this extent, Ānanda, it is sufficient to call a bhikkhu 'skilled in the elements.
"But to what extent, Bhante, is it sufficient to call a bhikkhu 'skilled in the sense bases'?"
“Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these six internal and external sense bases:
the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.
It is from these, Ānanda, that one knows and sees the six internal and external sense bases.”
“To this extent, Ānanda, it is sufficient to call a bhikkhu ‘skilled in the sense-bases.
But to what extent, Bhante, is it sufficient to call a bhikkhu ‘skilled in dependent origination’?
“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands thus:”
‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say:
with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.’
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises.
With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises.
With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
With the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness;
with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form;
with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases.
With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging;
with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence;
with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth.
With the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
It is to this extent, Ānanda, that it is appropriate to say, ‘A bhikkhu is skilled in dependent origination.’”
“But to what extent, Bhante, is it appropriate to say that a bhikkhu is ‘skilled in what is possible and what is impossible’?

“In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent—such a case does not exist.
He understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person might regard some conditioned phenomenon as permanent—such a case does exist.’”
He understands: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as pleasant;
such a case does not exist. He understands: "But it is possible that an ordinary person might regard some conditioned phenomenon as pleasant; such a case does exist. He understands:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any phenomenon as self; such a case does not exist."
He understands: "It is possible that an ordinary person might regard some phenomenon as a self; this possibility exists. He understands:
"It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person accomplished in view should deprive his mother of life;
such a possibility does not exist. He understands: "But it is possible that an ordinary person might deprive his mother of life; this possibility exists."
He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person accomplished in view should deprive his father of life … [or] should deprive an arahant of life; such a thing is possible.
He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person accomplished in view should, with a mind of hatred, draw the blood of a Tathāgata; such a thing is not possible.’
‘It is possible that an ordinary person, with a mind of ill will, might draw blood from a Tathāgata; it is possible,’ he understands.
‘It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a person possessed of right view to cause a schism in the Saṅgha; such a thing is not possible,’ he understands.
‘But it is possible that an ordinary person might cause a schism in the Saṅgha; it is possible,’ he understands.

He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view should name another teacher—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that an ordinary person might name another teacher—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, should arise in a single world-system—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Wheel-turning Monarchs should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Wheel-turning Monarch should arise in a single world-system—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Universal Monarchs should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Universal Monarch should arise in a single world-system—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a single world-system—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten thousand world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten thousand world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred thousand world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred thousand world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a million world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a million world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten million world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten million world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred million world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred million world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a billion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a billion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten billion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten billion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred billion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred billion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a trillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a trillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten trillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten trillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred trillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred trillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a quadrillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a quadrillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten quadrillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten quadrillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred quadrillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred quadrillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a quintillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a quintillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten quintillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten quintillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred quintillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred quintillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a sextillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a sextillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten sextillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten sextillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred sextillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred sextillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a septillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a septillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten septillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten septillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred septillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred septillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a quintillion-septillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a quintillion-septillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in ten quintillion-septillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in ten quintillion-septillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a hundred quintillion-septillion world-systems—such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that one Buddha should arise in a hundred quintillion-septillion world-systems—such a case exists. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Buddhas should arise simultaneously
‘It is possible that a single Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, might arise in a single world-system; this possibility exists,’ he understands.
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Wheel-turning Monarchs should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system; no such possibility exists,’ he understands.
‘But it is possible that a single Wheel-turning Monarch might arise in a single world-system; this possibility exists,’ he understands.
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a woman should be an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha; such a thing is not found,’ he understands.
‘But it is possible that a man should be an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha; such a thing is found,’ he understands.
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a woman should be a wheel-turning monarch; such a thing is not found,’ he understands.
He understands: ‘It is possible that a man might be a wheel-turning monarch; this is possible. He understands:
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a woman might exercise the role of Sakka... might exercise the role of Māra... might exercise the role of Brahmā;
this is not possible. He understands: ‘But it is possible that a man might exercise the role of Sakka... might exercise the role of Māra... might exercise the role of Brahmā; this is possible.’
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a desirable, pleasing, and agreeable result should arise from bodily misconduct; such a thing is not possible,’ he understands.
‘But it is possible that an undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable result should arise from bodily misconduct; such a thing is possible,’ he understands.
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a desirable, pleasing, and agreeable result should arise from verbal misconduct... [and so on].
He understands: ‘It is impossible that an agreeable, pleasing, and delightful result could arise from mental misconduct;

such a thing cannot exist. And he understands: ‘But it is possible that an disagreeable, unpleasing, and unpleasant result could arise from verbal misconduct... [and] from mental misconduct; such a thing can exist.’
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that an undesirable, unpleasing, or disagreeable result should arise from good conduct of body; such a thing is not found,’ he understands.
‘But it is possible that a desirable, pleasing, and agreeable result should arise from good conduct of body; such a thing is found,’ he understands.
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that an undesirable, unpleasing, or disagreeable result should arise from good conduct of speech... [and so on].
He understands: ‘It is impossible that an undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasant result should arise from mental good conduct’;
and he understands: ‘But it is possible that a desirable, lovely, and pleasant result should arise from verbal good conduct... [and] from mental good conduct; this is indeed possible.’

‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that one who has committed misconduct of body, on account of that and with that as condition, after the breakup of the body, after death, should reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world—such a case does not exist,’ he understands.

‘But it is possible, such a case exists, that one who has committed misconduct of body, on account of that and with that as condition, after the breakup of the body, after death, should reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell,’ he understands.
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that one who has committed misconduct of speech... [and so on].

He understands: ‘It is impossible that one who possesses misconduct of mind, on account of that and with that as condition, should, upon the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a good destination, a heavenly world—such a case does not exist. And he understands:
‘But it is possible that one who possesses misconduct of speech...

[and] one who possesses misconduct of mind, on account of that and with that as condition, should, upon the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell—such a case exists.’

‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that one who possesses good conduct of body, on account of that and with that as condition, after the breakup of the body, after death, should reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell—such a case does not exist,’ he understands.

‘But it is possible, such a case exists, that one who possesses good conduct of body, on account of that and with that as condition, after the breakup of the body, after death, should reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world—such a case exists,’ he understands.
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that one who possesses good conduct of speech …’ [and so on].

He understands: ‘It is impossible that one who possesses good conduct of mind, on account of that and with that as condition, should at the breaking up of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell;

no such case exists. And he understands: ‘But it is possible that one who possesses good conduct of speech … [and] one who possesses good conduct of mind, on account of that and with that as condition, should at the breaking up of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in the heavenly world; such a case exists.’
"To this extent, Ānanda, it is sufficient to say that a bhikkhu is 'skilled in what is possible and what is impossible.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
"It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!"
“What, Bhante, is the name of this Dhamma exposition?

“Therefore, Ānanda, you should remember this Dhamma exposition as ‘The Many Elements,’ and you should remember it as ‘The Fourfold Cycle,’ and you should remember it as ‘The Mirror of Dhamma,’ and you should remember it as ‘The Drum of the Deathless,’ and you should remember it as ‘The Unsurpassed’…”
“Also, ‘Victory in Battle,’ you should remember it by this name.
This is what the Blessed One said.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Bahudhātukasutta, the fifth, is finished.
